rw: Fees are taken from the invested balance every year, so less money stays working and the lost growth itself would have compounded, which widens the gap over decades.

ww.They always increase returns for the inv: Fees are a cost deducted from the account, so they lower the investor's net returns rather than raise them; they never add to what the investor earns.
ww.They have no effect after the first year: Fees such as expense ratios are charged every single year, not once, so their drag keeps growing as the balance compounds; the effect clearly continues after the first year.
ww.They make accounts risk-free for the inv: Fees do nothing to reduce risk; market investments stay risky no matter what is charged, and paying more does not make an account safe or guarantee any result.

rw: The expense ratio is the percentage of fund assets taken each year to cover management and operating costs, so it measures the yearly cost of owning that fund.

ww.The tax rate on all dividends: An expense ratio is a fund cost, not a tax rate; the tax on dividends is a separate charge set by the government and paid by the investor.
ww.The interest rate paid on a loan: An interest rate on a loan is what a borrower pays a lender; an expense ratio describes ongoing fund costs for investors, so the two are unrelated ideas.
ww.The ratio of debt to income owed: A debt to income ratio compares what a person owes with what they earn and is used by lenders; it has nothing to do with fund costs.

rw: Fund A charges only 0.05% against 1.0% for Fund B, so a far larger share of its money stays invested and compounds, leaving more at the end.

ww.Fund B, because higher fees mean better: Higher fees do not buy better results; charging 1.0% instead of 0.05% takes more from the balance each year, so Fund B would trail with other things equal.
ww.They will be identical in value at the e: The funds charge different fees, and a 0.95 point yearly gap compounds over many years, so their ending values would not be identical; Fund A would end ahead.
ww.Neither will grow at all over the next l: Both funds can still grow when markets rise, because fees only reduce returns and do not stop growth; neither fund is frozen, and Fund A simply grows more.

rw: A brokerage account is held at a firm and lets you buy and sell investments such as stocks, bonds and funds, which is exactly what defines it.

ww.An account for borrowing money from lend: Borrowing money from lenders happens through a loan or credit account; a brokerage account is used to hold and trade investments, not to take out loans.
ww.An account that guarantees a fixed retur: A brokerage account guarantees nothing; investments held in it can rise or fall in value, so no fixed return is promised to the account owner.
ww.An account used only to pay monthly bill: Paying monthly bills is the job of a checking account; a brokerage account is built for investing, so calling it bill-only gets its purpose wrong.

rw: A market order executes immediately at the best available current price, so the trade is almost sure to fill, though the exact price is not fixed in advance.

ww.An order that triggers only if a price f: That describes a stop order, which triggers once the price falls to a chosen level; a market order has no trigger price and simply executes right away.
ww.An order that cancels automatically at t: Canceling at the end of the day describes a day order's time limit, which is a duration setting; it says nothing about how or at what price a market order fills.
ww.An order to buy only at a set price or l: Buying only at a set price or lower describes a limit order; a market order does not wait for a price and accepts whatever the best current price is.

rw: A limit order sets a maximum buy price or minimum sell price, so it fills only at that price or better, which gives price control but no guarantee of filling.

ww.An order to trade at once at any price,: Trading at once at any price describes a market order; a limit order instead sets a price boundary and refuses to fill outside it.
ww.An order that cancels the account and en: A limit order does not close an account or end anything; it is an instruction to trade at a chosen price, and the account stays open after it.
ww.An order that waits for tax season to be: Brokers fill orders based on market prices and the order's limit, not tax season; tax timing has no connection to how a limit order works.

rw: A bull market is a period when prices are rising or expected to rise, usually with investor optimism, and the name is used for the broad upward trend.

ww.A market in which prices never change fo: A market where prices never change does not exist in practice; prices move constantly, and a bull market is defined by a clear upward trend, not by flat prices.
ww.A market in which prices are falling for: Prices falling for months describes a bear market, the opposite of a bull market, in which investors are pessimistic and stocks trend downward over time.
ww.A market closed for the whole season by: A bull market is not a closed market; exchanges keep trading on normal days, and the term describes the direction of prices rather than any closure.

rw: A bear market is a sustained fall in prices, commonly defined as a drop of 20% or more from a recent high, usually along with pessimism among investors.

ww.A market for wild animals and their pelt: The term is a figure of speech about price direction, not an actual market for animals or pelts; it names falling stock markets, so the literal reading fails.
ww.A market with no investors in it at all: A market always has investors, since prices come from buyers and sellers trading; a bear market has plenty of participants and simply sees falling prices.
ww.A market in which prices are rising stea: Steadily rising prices describe a bull market, which is the opposite of a bear market; a bear market is marked by a sharp and lasting decline.

rw: Selling everything in a panic at the low locks in losses and misses the later recovery, which is why it is the poor response for a long-term investor.

ww.Rebalancing to the target mix of your as: Rebalancing back to your target mix is a sound, disciplined response because it restores your intended risk level and often buys assets after they have fallen.
ww.Continuing the regular contributions at: Continuing regular contributions buys more shares when prices are low, which helps long-term investors through dollar cost averaging, so it is a good response rather than a poor one.
ww.Reviewing the plan calmly and with great: Calmly reviewing the plan is sensible because it checks goals and risk tolerance without emotion; it is a good habit during a drop, not a mistake.

rw: Volatility measures how much and how fast an investment's price swings up and down; higher volatility means larger swings and generally greater risk for the holder.

ww.How much dividend a stock pays each year: How much dividend a stock pays each year describes dividend yield or payout, which is income; volatility measures how much prices move, not what is paid out.
ww.How long a bond lasts before it ends: How long a bond lasts before it ends is its term or maturity; volatility is about price movement, so this definition mixes up two unrelated bond and market ideas.
ww.How high a fee is for the account: The fee charged for an account is a cost such as an expense ratio or account fee; volatility has nothing to do with fees and refers to price changes.

rw: Maturity is the date the bond ends, when the issuer repays the principal, also called face value, to the bondholder; interest payments usually stop at that point.

ww.The date interest rates change for the l: Interest rate changes are not what maturity means; a bond's rate is typically set when issued, and the maturity date marks repayment of principal instead.
ww.The date the buyer receives a tax refund: A tax refund relates to income tax filing with the government and has no connection to bonds; maturity is when the issuer repays the bond's principal.
ww.The date the bond is first sold to buyer: The date a bond is first sold is its issue date; maturity is the later date when the principal comes due, so this confuses the start with the end.

rw: When market rates rise, new bonds pay more than existing ones, so existing bonds with lower fixed coupons become less attractive and their prices fall.

ww.It is zero: Prices do not drop to zero when rates rise; existing bonds still pay their fixed coupons and repay principal, so they keep real value and only reprice downward.
ww.No change: Prices do change, because buyers compare older bonds' fixed payments with new higher-rate bonds, so existing bond prices adjust downward when rates go up.
ww.It rises: Prices fall rather than rise, since higher market rates make new bonds more attractive than older low-coupon bonds, so existing bonds lose value in the market.

rw: A Treasury bond is long-term debt issued by the U.S. federal government through the Treasury, backed by its full faith and credit, and pays interest until maturity.

ww.A stock issued by the government in a st: Stocks represent ownership in companies, not government borrowing; a Treasury bond is debt issued by the federal government, not a stock issued by any state.
ww.A bond issued by a city or a town counci: A bond issued by a city or town council is a municipal bond; Treasury bonds come from the U.S. federal government, which is a different issuer entirely.
ww.A bond issued by a small private company: Small private companies issue corporate bonds, not Treasury bonds; Treasuries are issued by the U.S. Treasury Department on behalf of the federal government.

rw: A municipal bond is issued by a state or local government to fund public projects like schools and roads, and its interest is often exempt from federal tax.

ww.A bond issued by a bank for its own lend: Banks issue their own debt securities, but those are not municipal bonds; municipal bonds are issued by public bodies such as states, cities and counties.
ww.A bond issued by the federal government: A bond issued by the federal government is a Treasury bond; municipal bonds come from state or local governments instead, which makes this the wrong issuer.
ww.A bond issued by a shopping mall or a st: Shopping malls and stores issue corporate debt, not municipal bonds; municipal bonds are sold only by state or local government bodies for public projects.

rw: A REIT is a company that owns, and often operates, income-producing real estate such as apartments and offices, and it pays most of its income to shareholders.

ww.A type of homeowners insurance for a hou: A REIT is an investment company, not an insurance product; homeowners insurance protects a house against damage, which is a different financial tool altogether.
ww.A tax on property owned by a person or f: A property tax is a levy charged by governments on owned real estate; a REIT is a company that owns property and returns income to its shareholders.
ww.A mortgage taken out for a home, repaid: A mortgage is a loan taken to buy a home and repaid over years; a REIT is an investment that holds property, so the two are different things.

rw: Holding one company's stock concentrates risk, since one bad event can hurt the whole position, while a diversified fund spreads that risk across many holdings.

ww.It is risk-free because the company is l: No stock is risk-free, even a large company's; share prices can fall sharply and companies can fail, so size does not remove the risk.
ww.It is safer than any bond or other asset: A single stock is not safer than every bond or asset; many bonds are far more stable, and a single company's price can swing widely.
ww.It is guaranteed to rise over time in va: No stock is guaranteed to rise; prices can drop or stay flat for years, and some companies fail entirely, so a rise cannot be promised.

rw: In a stock split, a company issues more shares and lowers the price per share proportionally, so each holder owns more shares but the total value stays the same.

ww.A company gives away half its profits ea: Giving away half the profits sounds like a dividend policy, not a split; a stock split changes the number of shares and the price per share, not profit.
ww.A company halves its workforce to cut co: Cutting the workforce in half is layoff or restructuring and has no connection to shares; a split only changes share count and price per share.
ww.A company merges with a rival firm in to: A merger is a combination of two companies, which is a separate event; a stock split just divides existing shares into more units at a lower price.

rw: An IPO is the first time a private company sells its shares to the public, listing them on a stock exchange so investors can then buy and trade them.

ww.A company paying a dividend to its holde: Paying a dividend distributes profit to current shareholders and happens after a company is already public; an IPO is the first sale of shares to the public.
ww.A company buying back its own shares fro: A company buying back its shares is a repurchase, which reduces shares outstanding; an IPO is instead the first time a company sells its shares to the public.
ww.A company filing for bankruptcy after lo: Filing for bankruptcy is a legal process for a company that cannot pay its debts and has nothing to do with selling shares to the public.

rw: The P/E ratio divides a stock's price by the company's earnings per share, showing how much investors pay for each dollar of profit the company earns.

ww.A fund's fees compared with its returns: Fees compared with returns would be a cost to performance idea for funds; the P/E ratio is specific to a stock's price and its earnings.
ww.A company's debt compared with its asset: Debt compared with assets and equity is a leverage ratio such as debt to equity; P/E involves stock price and earnings, not the company's debt load.
ww.A bond's price compared with its yearly: A bond's price compared with its interest rate relates to yield, not P/E; the price to earnings ratio is for stocks and uses earnings per share.

rw: P/E equals price divided by earnings per share, so $60 divided by $4 equals 15, meaning investors pay $15 for each $1 of yearly earnings.

ww.56: 56 comes from subtracting 4 from 60, but P/E is found by dividing price by earnings per share, and subtraction gives a meaningless number here.
ww.240: 240 comes from multiplying 60 by 4, but P/E is a division of price by earnings per share, so multiplying the two figures is the wrong operation.
ww.0.067: 0.067 comes from dividing 4 by 60, which flips the ratio; P/E divides price by earnings, so it is 60 divided by 4, not 4 divided by 60.

rw: Dividend yield is annual dividends per share divided by the share price, showing the income return from dividends alone, so a $2 dividend on a $50 stock is 4%.

ww.The company's profit margin on its sales: A company's profit margin on sales is net income over revenue, which measures profitability; dividend yield measures income paid to shareholders relative to the share price.
ww.The fund's yearly fees and expense costs: A fund's yearly fees and costs are called the expense ratio; dividend yield measures income paid out by a stock compared with its price.
ww.The share price divided by the earnings: Share price divided by earnings is the price to earnings ratio, not dividend yield; yield uses dividends paid per share on top, divided by the share price.

rw: A penny stock is a low-priced share, often under about five dollars, in a small company with limited trading, which makes it speculative and risky for investors.

ww.A stock issued only to children and teen: Penny stocks are open to any investor and are not limited to children or teens; the name refers to a low share price, not the buyer's age.
ww.A stock worth exactly one cent per share: A penny stock does not need to be worth exactly one cent; the term covers low-priced stocks in general, often priced up to a few dollars per share.
ww.A government bond that pays very low rat: A government bond is a debt security backed by a government, not a stock; penny stocks are shares of small companies and are considered high risk.

rw: Guaranteed high returns with no risk is a classic mark of fraud, because every real investment carries risk and higher returns require taking more risk, so be suspicious.

ww.Send your bank password to claim the pri: Sending a bank password to claim a prize hands a stranger access to your money; it is exactly how scammers steal funds, so never do it.
ww.Invest everything immediately before the: Rushing in before an offer ends is a pressure tactic used by scammers; investing everything quickly in a promised guarantee risks losing all your savings.
ww.Share it with all your friends right awa: Passing a likely scam to friends and family spreads the fraud and could cost them money; the right step is to avoid it and report it.

rw: A Ponzi scheme is a fraud that pays earlier investors with money from newer investors rather than real profits, and it collapses once new money runs out.

ww.A legal retirement plan paying savers hi: A Ponzi scheme is illegal and not a retirement plan; legitimate retirement plans do not promise unusually high returns paid from other participants' money.
ww.A government bond fund held by retail ba: A bond fund held by banks is a normal, regulated investment product; a Ponzi scheme is a criminal fraud and has no connection to government bonds.
ww.A bank loan program for small family fir: Small business loan programs are legitimate lending; a Ponzi scheme is a fraud that uses new investors' deposits to pay old investors and invests nothing real.

rw: Financial literacy is the knowledge and skills to manage money well, including budgeting, saving, investing and borrowing, so a person can make sound decisions.

ww.The ability to print money legally at ho: Printing money is illegal for individuals and is done by government mints and printers; financial literacy is about managing money wisely and has no link to printing it.
ww.The habit of spending without planning f: Spending without planning is the opposite of financial literacy, which stresses budgeting, saving and thinking ahead about goals instead of spending with no plan.
ww.The ability to read newspapers only, wit: Reading newspapers is general literacy and has no direct link to managing money; financial literacy means making informed decisions about earning, saving, spending and investing.

rw: Comparing prices, quality and features across sellers helps you find the best value for the money you spend, which is why it is a smart habit.

ww.It removes the need for a budget in any: A budget is still needed when you comparison shop; comparing prices helps stretch money within a budget but does not replace planning how much to spend.
ww.It requires you to buy the first item yo: Comparison shopping means checking several options before buying, so it does the opposite of forcing you to buy the first item you see.
ww.It guarantees the highest price for ever: Comparison shopping is meant to lower what you pay, not to guarantee the highest price; paying more than needed is exactly what shoppers try to avoid.

rw: Unit pricing states the cost per standard unit, such as per ounce or per pound, which lets shoppers compare different package sizes fairly on value.

ww.The tax on one purchase at the store cou: Sales tax is a percentage added to a purchase; unit pricing is the cost per measure of the product, such as per ounce, and excludes tax.
ww.The total price of a shopping trip at th: The total at the register is the sum of all items plus tax; unit pricing instead breaks down the price of one item per unit of measure.
ww.The delivery fee for a package sent by m: A delivery fee is a shipping charge added to some orders; unit pricing is about price per unit of measure and has nothing to do with delivery.

rw: Dividing $4.60 by 20 ounces gives $0.23 per ounce, which is lower than the 12-ounce box at $0.25 per ounce, so the larger box is the better unit price.

ww.They are exactly equal in unit cost: The two boxes are not equal: $3.00 divided by 12 is $0.25 per ounce, while $4.60 divided by 20 is $0.23 per ounce, so the costs differ.
ww.The 12-ounce box at $0.25 per ounce: The 12-ounce box does cost $0.25 per ounce, since $3.00 divided by 12 is 0.25, but that is higher than $0.23 for the 20-ounce box, so it is worse.
ww.It cannot be determined from the data: The data are enough, because dividing each price by its ounces gives $0.25 and $0.23 per ounce; unit prices can be computed and compared directly.

rw: Identity theft is using someone else's personal information, such as a name or Social Security number, without permission to commit fraud or other crimes for gain.

ww.Forgetting your own password for a site: Forgetting your own password is an everyday inconvenience that can be fixed by a reset; it is not theft, since no one else is using your identity.
ww.Sharing a photo with a friend on a phone: Sharing a photo with a friend is ordinary use of a phone and involves no stolen personal information, so it is not identity theft.
ww.Changing your own name legally through a: Legally changing your own name through a court is a lawful process you choose yourself; identity theft means someone else misuses your identity without your consent.

rw: Strong unique passwords limit damage from any one breach, and shredding documents with personal data stops dumpster thieves, so together they best protect your identity.

ww.Use the same password for every account: Reusing one password across accounts is risky, because one breach would expose all of them; that habit makes identity theft more likely, not less.
ww.Throw bank statements in the public tras: Bank statements hold account numbers and personal data, and throwing them intact in public trash lets thieves find them, so they should be shredded instead.
ww.Share your Social Security number freely: Giving out your Social Security number freely online invites theft, since scammers and weak sites can misuse it; it should only be shared when truly necessary.

rw: Unexpected texts asking for a PIN are typical phishing, so do not click; instead contact your bank using a phone number you already know is genuine.

ww.Reply with your account number and the f: Replying with your account number and password hands scammers what they need to drain your account; a real bank never asks for this by text.
ww.Click the link and enter the PIN right a: Clicking the link and entering your PIN gives the sender your credentials, which is how phishing works; the account is not truly locked and you risk theft.
ww.Forward the text to your friends and all: Forwarding the text to friends and family spreads the scam and puts them at risk too; the safe step is to avoid it and verify with your bank.

rw: A credit freeze restricts lenders from viewing your credit report, so thieves find it hard to open new accounts in your name, while your existing accounts continue.

ww.Raises your credit score by fifty points: A credit freeze does not change your score; it only blocks access to your report, so no points are added or removed by placing one.
ww.Erases your debts and removes them from: A freeze does not erase debts or remove entries from your records; what you owe stays on the report, but new lenders cannot view it.
ww.Cancels all your existing cards and clos: A freeze leaves your current cards and accounts open and working; it does not cancel anything, and it only limits new credit checks by lenders.

rw: Reviewing statements regularly lets you catch mistakes, unauthorized charges and fraud quickly, which makes it easier to dispute them within the time limits that apply.

ww.Only when you are applying for a loan or: Checking only when applying for credit means errors and fraud could go unnoticed for months; regular review is what catches problems early.
ww.Never, because banks are always correct: Banks can and do make errors, and fraudulent charges happen, so never checking statements is risky; you are the best check on your own accounts.
ww.Only once every ten years, if at all, on: Waiting ten years would let fraud and errors pile up and miss dispute deadlines; statements should be reviewed at least monthly to catch problems promptly.

rw: A tax refund is money the government returns when your payments or withholding during the year exceeded the tax you actually owed for that year.

ww.A loan from the government to you: A tax refund is not a loan; it is your own money returned after you paid more tax than you owed, and it does not need to be repaid.
ww.A fee for filing taxes late each year: A fee for filing late is a penalty, which is the opposite of a refund; a refund returns money to you rather than charging you extra.
ww.A bonus paid by your employer in cash: An employer bonus is extra pay from your job and is taxed as income; a tax refund comes from the government and returns overpaid tax.

rw: The W-4 tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck, based on your filing status, dependents and other details you provide.

ww.Claiming a refund from the tax office ea: A refund is claimed by filing a tax return, not a W-4; the W-4 is given to your employer to set withholding from your paychecks.
ww.Reporting your yearly wages to the IRS a: Reporting yearly wages to the IRS is done with a W-2 that employers prepare; the W-4 is filled out by the employee at the start of work.
ww.Applying for a credit card at a bank bra: Credit card applications are made directly with a bank or card issuer; the W-4 is a tax withholding form for employees and is not used for credit.

rw: Gross pay is the total amount earned before any taxes or deductions are taken out, so it is the full figure from wages, salary or hours worked.

ww.Pay for overtime only, not regular hours: Overtime pay is only one part of earnings; gross pay includes regular hours, overtime and other pay together, so it is not limited to extra hours.
ww.Pay received only from tips and gratuiti: Tips and gratuities are one kind of income; gross pay covers all earnings combined, so limiting it to tips leaves out wages and salary.
ww.Pay after all taxes and deductions are t: Pay after all taxes and deductions is net pay, or take-home pay; gross pay is the amount before those subtractions, so this describes the opposite.

rw: Net pay is gross pay minus taxes and deductions, so $1,000 minus $150 minus $50 equals $800, the amount the worker actually takes home.

ww.$200: $200 is just the sum of the taxes and deductions ($150 plus $50); net pay is what remains after subtracting them from the $1,000 gross, not the amount taken.
ww.$850: $850 subtracts only the $150 in taxes and forgets the $50 in other deductions; both must be taken from gross pay, so $1,000 minus $200 is $800.
ww.$1,200: $1,200 adds the $200 of taxes and deductions to gross pay, which is the wrong direction; net pay must be lower than gross pay, not higher.

rw: Consumer rights include being informed about products and prices and being protected from deception, unsafe goods and unfair practices, which keeps markets fair for buyers.

ww.The right to avoid every tax on goods an: Consumers cannot avoid every tax; taxes apply by law, and consumer rights deal with fair treatment and protection from deception, not tax exemption.
ww.The right to ignore all store policies a: Consumers must follow store policies and contract terms they agree to, so there is no right to ignore them; the law protects against unfair terms instead.
ww.The right to buy anything for free in a: No law gives consumers a right to free goods; a consumer right is about fair treatment, such as honest information and safety, when you buy.

rw: The CFPB is a federal agency created to supervise banks and lenders and to protect consumers in loans, credit cards and other financial products and services.

ww.The National Park Service, a federal age: The National Park Service manages parks and historic sites and has no role in financial consumer protection, so it is not the agency asked about.
ww.The Federal Aviation Administration, for: The Federal Aviation Administration regulates air travel and aircraft safety, not financial products, so it does not protect consumers in the financial marketplace.
ww.The Postal Service, a federal mail agenc: The Postal Service delivers mail and packages and is not a financial regulator, so it does not oversee banks or protect financial consumers.

rw: Contacting the card issuer right away lets you report the fraud, block the card and dispute the charge, and prompt reports limit your liability.

ww.Pay it to avoid any more trouble: Paying an unauthorized charge confirms it and may make it harder to recover your money; you should dispute it first rather than just paying to be done.
ww.Ignore it and hope it fixes itself: Ignoring the charge leaves the thief free to charge more and can pass the dispute deadline, so hoping it fixes itself is a risky choice.
ww.Cancel your internet service plan: Cancelling internet service does nothing about the fraudulent card charge, since the problem is with the card account; the card issuer must be contacted instead.

rw: Reading the fine print means carefully reviewing all terms, fees, penalties and conditions in a contract before you agree, so you know what you commit to.

ww.Skipping the terms to save time, as all: Skipping the terms is the opposite of reading the fine print, and contracts are not all alike; fees and obligations differ, so skipping may cost you later.
ww.Signing without reading the contract fir: Signing without reading is what the fine print warning is meant to prevent, because you could agree to costs or duties you never noticed.
ww.Memorizing only the title of the contrac: Memorizing only the title tells you nothing about fees, penalties or duties, which are in the body of the contract, so it is not reading it.

rw: A warranty is a promise from the seller or maker to repair or replace a product that turns out to be defective within a stated period.

ww.A guarantee that the price will never ri: A warranty does not freeze prices; it covers defects or repairs, and sellers can still raise prices in the future, so no price guarantee exists.
ww.A tax on products sold in the stores of: A tax on products is levied by governments; a warranty is a promise from the maker or seller about the product's quality, not a tax.
ww.A rule that stops you from returning any: A warranty gives you protection and does not stop returns; return rules come from store or legal policy, and a warranty only adds repair or replacement coverage.

rw: Needs are essentials like food, housing and basic clothing, while wants are things that are nice to have but not required, so the line is about necessity.

ww.Needs are always luxury items for the ri: Needs are essentials, not luxury items; luxuries are wants, so claiming that needs are luxuries for the rich reverses the true meaning.
ww.Wants are always cheaper than needs in a: A want is not automatically cheaper than a need, since luxuries often cost more; the difference is about necessity, not price, so this claim is false.
ww.There is no difference between them at a: There is a clear difference, because needs are required to live and work, while wants are optional, and separating them is key to good budgeting.

rw: Impulse buying is purchasing something you did not plan to buy because of a sudden urge or emotion, often without weighing the cost or need.

ww.Purchasing only what is on a written lis: Buying only what is on a written list is planned buying, which is the opposite of impulse buying; an impulse purchase is not planned beforehand.
ww.Comparing prices carefully at several st: Comparing prices carefully across stores is deliberate shopping, so it is the opposite of an impulse purchase made without any thought.
ww.Waiting a week before buying anything th: Waiting a week before buying is a cooling off tactic that prevents impulse buying; it is a remedy for the habit and not a description of it.

rw: Waiting 24 hours gives the urge time to fade so you can judge whether you truly need the item, which cuts impulse buying effectively.

ww.Skipping the budget and spending money m: Skipping the budget and spending freely encourages impulse buying, since nothing limits you or reminds you of priorities; it makes the habit stronger.
ww.Shopping when you are bored or feeling i: Shopping when bored or in a bad mood raises the chance of emotional spending, so it increases impulse buys instead of reducing them.
ww.Keeping stored card details on every sho: Keeping card details stored on every site makes buying quick and effortless, which removes friction that might otherwise stop an impulse purchase.

rw: A cooling-off period is a set time after signing or buying, often a few days, when you can cancel the deal without penalty under certain laws.

ww.A time when prices are lowered for all: Lowered prices for all describes a sale or discount; a cooling-off period is a set time after a purchase during which a buyer can cancel.
ww.A time when stores close for repairs: Stores closing for repairs is a business shutdown for maintenance; a cooling-off period is a legal window to cancel a purchase, so they are unrelated.
ww.A time when interest is waived for you: Waived interest describes an introductory or grace offer on credit; a cooling-off period gives buyers a limited time to cancel a contract after agreeing.

rw: Tracking income and spending shows where your money actually goes, which gives the facts needed to set realistic limits and goals in a budget.

ww.Cut all spending at once with no review: Cutting all spending at once without reviewing past bills is guesswork and hard to sustain; a budget starts with knowing what you actually spend.
ww.Guess the numbers and never check them l: Guessing numbers and never checking them makes a budget unreliable, since real spending may differ widely, so it cannot guide good decisions.
ww.Open several new credit cards at the sam: Opening several new credit cards invites more debt and does nothing to show where your money goes, so it is not a first step in building a budget.

rw: A sinking fund is money set aside regularly in small amounts for a known future expense, such as car repairs, so the cost does not strain your budget.

ww.A fee charged by banks for opening new a: A fee charged for opening accounts is a bank cost, not a sinking fund; a sinking fund is money you save yourself toward a planned expense.
ww.A fund that loses value every year as it: A fund that loses value as it is spent on fees describes a poor investment; a sinking fund is money set aside on purpose for a future cost.
ww.A loan from a relative to pay for a big: A loan from a relative is borrowed money that must be repaid; a sinking fund is your own savings built up ahead of time for a purchase.

rw: Setting aside a fixed amount each month for a known future expense like car repairs is a sinking fund, which spreads the cost over time.

ww.Compound debt: Compound debt means debt that grows through interest on interest; setting aside $50 monthly is saving, not borrowing, so this term does not fit.
ww.A tax deduction: A tax deduction lowers taxable income at filing time; saving $50 each month for repairs is a planning habit and not a tax matter.
ww.Impulse buying: Impulse buying is an unplanned purchase on a sudden urge; the family is planning ahead for a known expense, so this is the opposite.

rw: Overdraft happens when you spend more than your checking balance holds, so the bank covers the shortfall, often charging a fee and leaving a negative balance.

ww.Saving more than planned in a given mont: Saving more than planned is a positive result and not an overdraft; overdraft involves spending beyond what the account holds, not putting extra money aside.
ww.Closing an account at a bank for good th: Closing an account is a separate step the customer chooses; overdraft is the shortfall from spending more than the balance, not the end of an account.
ww.Earning interest on savings, added to th: Earning interest on savings is a gain added to a balance, while overdraft is a negative situation where withdrawals exceed the money actually in the account.

rw: Low-balance alerts warn you before the account runs short, and tracking spending keeps you aware of the balance, which helps you avoid overdraft fees.

ww.Ignore the account until the monthly sta: Ignoring the account until the statement arrives lets the balance run low unnoticed, which makes overdrafts and fees more likely, not less.
ww.Write checks without checking the balanc: Writing checks without checking the balance risks spending money that is not there, and bounced items bring overdraft fees, so it increases the problem.
ww.Lend money to friends from the account o: Lending money from the account often can drain the balance below what is needed for bills and checks, which raises the risk of overdraft fees.

rw: A certificate of deposit holds money for a fixed term, such as two years, at a guaranteed rate and is insured, which suits money you will not need.

ww.A credit card balance owed: A credit card balance is money you owe, not a place to hold savings; it charges interest and cannot earn a guaranteed rate for you.
ww.A lottery ticket bought: A lottery ticket is gambling with no guaranteed return and a very low chance of winning, so it does not fit money meant to earn a guaranteed rate.
ww.A checking account fund: A checking account is for daily spending and usually pays little or no interest with no fixed rate, so it does not guarantee a rate for two years.

rw: The five Cs of credit are character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions, the factors lenders weigh when judging whether a borrower will repay a loan.

ww.Cash, coupons, cards, checks and coins,: Cash, coupons, cards, checks and coins are ways to pay, not lender criteria; the five Cs are factors lenders weigh when deciding whether to approve credit.
ww.Cost, color, class, cap and charge of th: Cost, color, class, cap and charge are not recognized credit factors; the five Cs lenders use have names tied to the borrower's reliability and finances.
ww.Credit, cost, cut, cap and cure for the: Credit, cost, cut, cap and cure is not the lender framework; the true list names traits like character and capacity that judge a borrower's ability to repay.

rw: Capacity is the borrower's ability to repay, judged by comparing income with existing debts, which matches the lender reviewing income and debts for affordability.

ww.Character: Character is about the borrower's reputation and repayment history, shown in credit reports; it does not mean reviewing income and debts to check whether payments are affordable.
ww.Conditions: Conditions cover the loan's purpose, terms and the wider economy, not the borrower's income and debts, so this does not describe an affordability review.
ww.Collateral: Collateral is an asset pledged to secure the loan, not a review of income and debts, so it does not describe checking whether payments are affordable.

rw: Collateral is property, such as a car or home, pledged to secure a loan, which the lender may take if the borrower fails to repay.

ww.A credit report from a bureau: A credit report from a bureau is a record of your borrowing history; collateral is property pledged to secure a loan, which is a different thing.
ww.A fee for late payments on a loan: A fee for late payments is a penalty charged for missing a due date; collateral is an asset that backs a loan and may be seized if unpaid.
ww.The interest rate charged on a loan: The interest rate is the price of borrowing money; collateral is an asset pledged as security, so it is not a rate or a cost.

rw: A secured loan is backed by collateral, such as a car or house, which the lender can claim if the borrower fails to repay, often giving lower rates.

ww.A loan with no repayment: A loan with no repayment would be a gift; a secured loan must be repaid and is simply backed by collateral that protects the lender.
ww.A loan only for businesses: Secured loans are made to individuals and businesses alike, so they are not limited to businesses; the key feature is the collateral behind the loan.
ww.A loan guaranteed by luck: Luck guarantees nothing in lending; a secured loan is backed by specific collateral that the lender can take, so this wording makes no sense.

rw: Credit utilization is the percentage of your available credit that you are currently using, found by dividing balances by total limits, and lower is generally better for scores.

ww.The number of credit cards owned by the: The number of cards you own is a count and not a ratio; credit utilization compares the balances you carry with your available credit limits.
ww.The yearly fee on a card charged by the: A yearly card fee is a charge from the issuer; utilization is a ratio of balances to limits, so a fee is unrelated.
ww.The interest rate on a card charged to t: The interest rate on a card is the APR and is the cost of carrying a balance; utilization measures how much of your limit you use.

rw: Utilization is balances divided by limits, so $3,000 divided by $10,000 equals 0.30, or 30%, meaning the borrower uses three tenths of available credit.

ww.3%: 3% would result from $300 on $10,000, but $3,000 over $10,000 is 0.30, so the decimal point is misplaced by a factor of ten here.
ww.300%: 300% would mean balances far above the limits, but $3,000 is only part of $10,000, so the ratio is 0.30 or 30%, not 300%.
ww.70%: 70% is the share of credit still unused ($7,000 of $10,000), not the share used; utilization measures the used portion, which is 30%.

rw: A hard inquiry appears when a lender checks your credit report while considering your application for credit, and it can slightly lower your score for a time.

ww.You checked your own credit; the check i: Checking your own credit is a soft inquiry, which does not affect your score, so this describes a soft pull and not a hard inquiry.
ww.You closed a bank account at the branch: Closing a bank account is not recorded as a hard inquiry; inquiries come only from credit report requests made by lenders and similar parties.
ww.You paid a bill early and got a discount: Paying a bill early may help your payment history but creates no inquiry; hard inquiries arise only when a lender checks your credit for an application.

rw: A cosigner legally agrees to pay if the borrower does not, so when the student stops paying, the parent must repay the loan and may see credit damage.

ww.Nobody but the bank itself: The bank is certainly owed the money, but it can collect from the cosigner who agreed to guarantee the loan, so it is not the only party responsible.
ww.Only the bank and no one else: The bank is the lender and not the one who repays; a cosigner legally promised to pay if the student stops, so someone else is also responsible.
ww.The government as guarantor: The government is not a guarantor on a private student loan cosigned by a parent; the cosigner is the person who guaranteed repayment.

rw: A common target is three to six months of expenses, so $2,000 times 3 is $6,000 and times 6 is $12,000, giving the range $6,000 to $12,000.

ww.$600 to $1,500 total: $600 to $1,500 is less than one month of expenses ($2,000), well short of the common three to six month target for an emergency fund.
ww.$2,000,000 in reserve: $2,000,000 is a thousand months of expenses, far beyond an emergency reserve; the goal is a few months of costs, not a huge fortune.
ww.$0 to $100 only: $0 to $100 would not cover even a day or two of $2,000 monthly expenses, so it is far below any sensible emergency fund target.

rw: Index funds usually charge very low fees and hold many securities, which spreads risk, and these two traits make them popular with long-term investors.

ww.Guaranteed returns on every fund: No fund can guarantee returns; index funds follow the market, so their value can rise or fall, and a promise of guaranteed returns is false.
ww.No exposure to markets, cash only: Index funds invest in markets such as stocks or bonds, so they have exposure to market ups and downs; they are not cash only.
ww.Daily large profits for investors: Index funds do not deliver large daily profits; they track a market and can fall as well as rise, and they aim for steady long-term growth.

rw: A 50% match on the first 6% means free money, so contributing at least 6% to capture the full match gives an instant return on your savings.

ww.Skip it to avoid saving any money at all: Skipping the match means turning down free employer money; avoiding saving at all this year gives up both your savings and the matching contribution.
ww.Contribute nothing and invest later when: Contributing nothing now and investing later wastes the match you could get each year and loses years of compounding, so the delay costs you.
ww.Withdraw it each year to spend it on you: Withdrawing the money each year to spend it loses the match benefit's long-term growth and can bring taxes and penalties, defeating the plan's purpose.

rw: A Roth IRA is funded with after-tax dollars, so the money grows tax-free and qualified withdrawals in retirement are not taxed, subject to the rules.

ww.A checking account used for daily bills: A checking account is used for daily bills and everyday spending; a Roth IRA is a retirement account that holds long-term savings and investments.
ww.A savings bond issued by the federal gov: A savings bond is a government debt product sold at a discount or face value; a Roth IRA is a retirement account, not a bond.
ww.A type of insurance policy sold to peopl: Insurance policies protect against loss and are not retirement accounts; a Roth IRA is open to working people of many ages and holds investments for retirement.

rw: A higher deductible means you accept more of the cost of a claim, so the insurer takes less risk and charges a lower premium.

ww.It disappears: Premiums do not vanish with a higher deductible; you still pay for coverage, so a higher deductible only reduces the cost, and does not remove it.
ww.It increases: The premium goes down rather than up with a higher deductible, because the insurer expects to pay less on claims, so an increase would be backwards.
ww.It stays put: The premium usually changes with the deductible, since the insurer's risk shifts when you bear more cost; it falls with a higher deductible.

rw: Renters insurance typically covers your personal belongings from events like fire or theft and liability if someone is hurt or you damage property in the rented home.

ww.Rent payments only, not the landlord's o: Renters insurance does not pay your rent; it covers your belongings and liability, and the landlord's building is insured under the landlord's own policy.
ww.Car repairs after any crash on a public: Car repairs after a crash fall under auto insurance, which is a separate policy; renters insurance protects belongings and liability inside a rented home.
ww.The building itself and the land under t: The landlord's own policy covers the building and land; renters insurance does not, because you do not own either one.

rw: Liability insurance pays for injury or property damage you cause to others and covers legal costs if you are sued, protecting your own finances from such claims.

ww.A warranty on a product you buy in a sho: A warranty relates to repairs of a purchased product and is not insurance; liability insurance covers claims against you for harm you cause to others.
ww.A savings account for lawsuits and legal: A savings account holds money you choose to set aside; liability insurance is a policy that pays when you are legally responsible for harming others.
ww.Coverage for your own injuries only, non: Covering only your own injuries describes health or personal injury cover; liability insurance pays for harm or damage you cause to other people.

rw: Liability coverage pays for damage and injuries you cause to others, so it pays for the repair of the other driver's car in a crash you cause.

ww.Comprehensive coverage: Comprehensive coverage pays for non-collision damage to your own car, like theft or storms, and does not pay for the other driver's car.
ww.Collision coverage: Collision coverage pays to repair your own car after a crash, not the other driver's vehicle, so it does not cover the damage you cause to them.
ww.Health coverage: Health coverage pays medical bills for injuries and does not pay for repairs to vehicles, so it would not cover the other driver's car.

rw: A tax deduction reduces your taxable income, so you pay tax on a smaller amount, and the savings equal the deduction times your tax rate.

ww.A penalty for late filing of a tax retur: A penalty for late filing is an added cost, not a deduction; a deduction lowers the income on which you are taxed, so this is the opposite.
ww.A dollar-for-dollar cut in the tax you o: A dollar-for-dollar cut in tax owed describes a tax credit; a deduction only lowers taxable income, so it saves less than its full amount.
ww.An extra charge on income earned by work: An extra charge on income is a tax or surcharge; a deduction does the reverse by lowering the income that gets taxed.

rw: A tax credit reduces the tax you owe directly, dollar for dollar, so a $1,000 credit lowers your tax bill by exactly $1,000.

ww.A penalty on earnings above a certain li: A penalty on earnings above a limit is a charge, while a credit is a benefit that reduces your tax bill; the two are opposite.
ww.An amount that lowers taxable income bef: Lowering taxable income describes a deduction; a credit instead subtracts straight from the tax owed, which makes it generally more valuable than a deduction.
ww.A loan from the government to taxpayers: A government loan must be repaid; a tax credit is a reduction in tax that never has to be paid back, so it is not a loan.

rw: A credit subtracts directly from tax owed, saving the full $1,000, while a deduction at a 22% rate saves only $220, so the credit saves more.

ww.Neither saves: Both reduce taxes, so saying neither saves anything is wrong; a $1,000 credit cuts tax by $1,000, and a deduction cuts it by only a portion of $1,000.
ww.Both save equally: They do not save equally, since a deduction only reduces taxable income and saves tax at your rate, such as $220 at 22%, while a credit saves $1,000.
ww.The $1,000 deduction: A $1,000 deduction saves just your tax rate times $1,000, for instance $220 at 22%, which is less than the $1,000 a credit saves.

rw: In a progressive tax, higher incomes face higher rates, as in the U.S. federal income tax brackets, so people with more income pay a larger percentage.

ww.A tax paid only by the poor and the midd: A progressive tax is not limited to the poor and middle class; it charges higher rates as income rises, so wealthier people pay a larger share.
ww.A tax with no rate set by any law at all: Tax rates are always set by law, so a tax with no legal rate is not a real tax; a progressive tax has rates that rise with income.
ww.A tax with the same rate for every taxpa: The same rate for everyone is a flat tax; a progressive tax uses higher rates for higher income brackets, so equal rates do not fit.

rw: A sales tax is the same rate on purchases, which takes a larger share of income from low earners than high earners, so it is regressive.

ww.Estate tax: An estate tax falls on the value of a large inheritance and is paid mainly by wealthy estates, so it is progressive rather than regressive.
ww.Gift tax: A gift tax applies to large gifts, mostly by wealthier people, and rises with value, so it is not regressive and takes a bigger share from wealth.
ww.Income tax: The federal income tax uses brackets with higher rates at higher income, so it is progressive, not regressive; a regressive tax takes more from low incomes.

rw: FICA is the payroll tax withheld from wages that pays for Social Security and Medicare, with both employees and employers contributing a share of it.

ww.A sales tax charged in shops on goods an: A sales tax is charged on purchases in shops; FICA is instead withheld from paychecks, so a retail tax is not what it describes.
ww.A tax on gifts given from one person to: A tax on gifts is the gift tax; FICA is a payroll tax on wages, so this describes a different federal levy altogether.
ww.A tax on real estate owned by a person o: A tax on real estate is a property tax collected locally; FICA is a payroll tax withheld from earnings, so land and buildings are not involved.

rw: Strong unique passwords stop one breach from exposing every account, and monitoring accounts helps you spot unusual activity early, together lowering your risk of identity theft.

ww.Sharing your passwords with friends and: Sharing passwords with others gives them access to your accounts and raises the risk of misuse, so it makes identity theft easier rather than protecting you.
ww.Ignoring bank statements for several mon: Ignoring statements for months lets fraud grow unnoticed and can pass dispute deadlines; watching your accounts is a main way to detect identity theft.
ww.Using one simple password everywhere so: One simple password everywhere is easy to guess and means a single breach exposes all your accounts, which makes identity theft more likely.

rw: Phishing emails try to steal your password, so avoid the link and contact the company by a trusted number or website you already know is real.

ww.Forward it to friends and all of your co: Forwarding the email to coworkers spreads a phishing scam and puts others at risk; the right step is to avoid it and verify with the company.
ww.Reply with your card number and the secu: Replying with a card number and security code hands a scammer what is needed to charge your card, so never share these details by email.
ww.Click and enter your password so the acc: Entering your password on a link from an unexpected email sends it straight to scammers, who can then take over your account.

rw: The CFPB protects consumers in financial products and services such as mortgages, credit cards and loans by enforcing rules and handling complaints about unfair practices.

ww.Sets the federal budget and decides what: Setting the federal budget is done by Congress and the President; the CFPB focuses on financial consumer protection and does not decide what the government spends.
ww.Prints money and coins for use by the wh: Printing money and coins is done by the Treasury's bureaus and the Federal Reserve; the CFPB does not make currency, and it supervises financial firms.
ww.Runs the stock market and sets prices of: Running the stock market and setting share prices is not a government job; prices come from trading, and the SEC, not the CFPB, oversees securities markets.

rw: Federal law lets you request a free credit report from each of the major bureaus on a regular schedule, so you can check them for errors without paying.

ww.You receive cash payments for the report: Bureaus do not pay you for your reports; the right is to see your own information free of charge, not to receive money for it.
ww.Only banks can see them, and not the per: You are entitled to see your own report, not only banks or lenders; checking it helps you find errors or fraud affecting you.
ww.You must pay for every report that you r: Free reports are available to you under the law, so you are not required to pay for each one; paying is not mandatory for the annual copy.

rw: An account you never opened suggests identity theft or an error, and disputing it with the bureau and the creditor starts the process of getting it removed.

ww.Pay it to be safe and avoid any more tro: Paying a debt that is not yours can be treated as accepting it and wastes money, so you should dispute it instead of paying to avoid trouble.
ww.Close all your accounts at the bank and: Closing your own accounts does nothing to remove the unknown account and harms your credit history; the problem is the false entry that must be disputed.
ww.Ignore it because it will vanish by itse: Ignoring a false account lets damage to your credit continue and may lead to collections; errors do not vanish by themselves and must be disputed.

rw: Net pay, or take-home pay, is the amount of wages left after taxes and other deductions have been subtracted from gross pay.

ww.Total earnings before deductions, shown: Total earnings before deductions is gross pay, which is shown on a pay stub; net pay is the smaller amount you receive after deductions.
ww.The yearly tax bill owed to the state re: The yearly tax bill is the total tax owed to the state; net pay is the paycheck amount that remains after taxes and deductions come out.
ww.The cost of benefits only, paid for by t: The cost of benefits only paid by an employer is a business expense; net pay is the money an employee takes home after taxes and deductions.

rw: Net pay equals gross pay minus deductions, so $2,000 minus $450 equals $1,550, the amount the worker actually takes home each pay period.

ww.$450: $450 is only the total of the deductions; net pay is what remains after subtracting them from gross pay, so $2,000 minus $450 is $1,550.
ww.$1,000: $1,000 does not match the data; subtracting $450 from $2,000 gives $1,550, so $1,000 would require deductions of $1,000, not $450.
ww.$2,450: $2,450 adds the deductions to gross pay, which is the wrong direction; net pay must be lower than the $2,000 gross, not higher.

rw: A zero-based budget gives every dollar of income a purpose, such as bills, savings or fun, so income minus planned spending equals zero with nothing left unassigned.

ww.A budget with no spending at all, so all: A budget with no spending at all, saving all income, is not zero-based; zero-based budgeting plans to use every dollar, including savings, so the budget balances to zero.
ww.A budget with zero savings, so every dol: A zero-based budget does not demand zero savings; savings are one of the jobs a dollar can get, so spending everything on wants and needs is wrong.
ww.A budget with no income, so the plan sho: A zero-based budget starts from your income and assigns it all; having no income would leave nothing to assign, so a plan showing only bills is not zero-based.

rw: The envelope method puts a set amount of cash for each spending category, such as food or fun, into its own envelope, so once empty you stop spending.

ww.Saving all money in one account so the b: Keeping all money in one account is the opposite of dividing it by category; the envelope method separates funds, so one combined balance does not match it.
ww.Using only credit cards for all of your: The envelope method uses cash, not credit cards; relying on cards removes the physical limit that makes envelope budgeting work for controlling spending.
ww.Mailing bills early to the companies tha: Mailing bills early is a bill payment habit and is not budgeting by envelope; the envelope method is about dividing cash among spending categories.

rw: In the 50/30/20 rule, 20% goes to savings and debt repayment, and 20% of $3,200 is 0.20 times 3,200, which equals $640.

ww.$960: $960 is 30% of $3,200 and is the wants share; under 50/30/20 savings and debt repayment get 20%, which is smaller than $960.
ww.$1,600: $1,600 is 50% of $3,200 and covers needs; savings and debt repayment receive only 20% in the 50/30/20 rule, which is less than that.
ww.$320: $320 is 10% of $3,200, but the 50/30/20 rule gives savings and debt repayment 20%, so $320 is half the correct amount.

rw: Wants get 30% under the 50/30/20 rule, and 30% of $3,200 is 0.30 times 3,200, which equals $960 for wants.

ww.$1,200: $1,200 would be 37.5% of $3,200, which is not a share in the 50/30/20 rule; wants get 30%, so the figure is incorrect.
ww.$1,600: $1,600 is 50% of $3,200 and goes to needs; wants receive only 30% in the 50/30/20 rule, which is $960.
ww.$640: $640 is 20% of $3,200 and is the savings and debt portion; wants get 30%, which is the larger amount of $960.

rw: Monthly rent is the same amount each month under a lease, so it is a fixed expense that you can plan for easily.

ww.Gasoline: Gasoline use changes with how much you drive and with price swings, so the amount differs from month to month and is a variable expense.
ww.Electric bill: An electric bill depends on how much power you use and changes by season, so it is a variable expense rather than a fixed one.
ww.Dining out: Dining out changes with how often you eat out and what you order, so the spending varies and is a flexible, variable expense.

rw: Groceries vary with how much you buy and with prices, so the amount changes from month to month, which makes them a variable expense.

ww.Car loan: A car loan has a set payment each month for the length of the loan, so it is a fixed expense, not a variable one.
ww.Insurance: Insurance premiums are usually a set amount on a regular schedule, so they are fixed expenses, even if billed monthly or yearly.
ww.Gym fees: Gym fees are normally the same each month under a membership, which makes them a fixed expense rather than a variable one.

rw: Disposable income is the money left after income taxes are paid, which you can then spend on needs and wants or save.

ww.Income before taxes and fees: Income before taxes and fees is gross income, the full amount earned; disposable income is what remains after taxes have been paid.
ww.Income from investments only: Investment income is just one possible source of earnings; disposable income is any income left over after taxes, whatever its source.
ww.Income after rent and food paid: Income left after rent and food is discretionary income, a narrower idea; disposable income is defined as what remains after taxes, before necessary spending.

rw: Gross income is the total earned from wages and other sources before taxes and deductions are subtracted, so it is the highest income figure.

ww.Pay received after taxes are taken out: Pay received after taxes are taken out is net income, or take-home pay; gross income is the larger amount before those taxes and deductions.
ww.Money saved in a bank account each year: Money saved in a bank account is a savings balance; gross income is what you earn before taxes, so saving is a different concept.
ww.Interest owed on a loan to the lender: Interest owed on a loan is a borrowing cost that you pay to a lender; gross income is what you earn, not what you owe.

rw: Net income is the pay that remains after taxes and deductions are subtracted from gross income, which is the take-home amount you can budget with.

ww.Total savings at the end of the year: Total savings at year end is an accumulated balance; net income describes pay after taxes and deductions, so savings are a different idea.
ww.Pay before deductions, the total earned: Pay before deductions is gross income, the total earned; net income is the smaller figure that remains once taxes and deductions are taken out.
ww.Total spending over the whole of the yea: Total spending over a year is your expenses; net income measures what you earn after taxes, not what you spend.

rw: Net pay is gross pay minus deductions, so $2,000 minus $460 equals $1,540, the amount Jordan takes home each pay period.

ww.$1,460: $1,460 does not match the arithmetic; $2,000 minus $460 equals $1,540, so $1,460 comes from a subtraction slip that swaps the last two digits.
ww.$2,460: $2,460 adds the deductions to gross pay, which is the wrong direction; net pay must be lower than the $2,000 gross, not higher.
ww.$460: $460 is only the amount of the deductions; net pay is what remains after taking them from gross pay, which is $2,000 minus $460.

rw: Income, expenses and goals shift over time, so a budget must be reviewed and updated regularly to remain realistic and useful.

ww.To increase bank fees on your accounts: Reviewing a budget does not raise bank fees; the aim is to keep your plan current so spending matches your real income and goals.
ww.To avoid saving any money at all later: Reviewing a budget helps you save more by showing where money goes; it does not help you avoid saving, so this reason is backwards.
ww.Budgets never need changes once written: Budgets do need changes, because income, prices and goals change; a plan written once and never updated will soon stop matching your life.

rw: Dividing the $1,200 goal by 8 months gives $150 per month, and $150 times 8 equals $1,200, which meets the goal exactly.

ww.$200: $200 per month for 8 months totals $1,600, which is more than the $1,200 needed; the monthly amount should be $1,200 divided by 8.
ww.$96: $96 per month for 8 months totals only $768, which falls short of $1,200; dividing $1,200 by 8 gives the needed monthly amount.
ww.$1,200: $1,200 is the full goal and would mean saving everything in one month; spreading it over 8 months means setting aside $150 each month.

rw: Pay yourself first means moving money into savings right when you are paid, before spending on anything else, so saving is treated as a priority.

ww.Borrowing money in order to build up you: Borrowing to build up savings creates debt and interest costs that cancel out the benefit; pay yourself first uses your own income for saving.
ww.Paying bills late in order to keep more: Paying bills late is harmful, with fees and credit damage; pay yourself first means saving at the start, not delaying bills to keep cash.
ww.Spending first and saving what is left o: Spending first and saving what is left over is the opposite order, and often leaves nothing to save, which pay yourself first aims to prevent.

rw: Living beyond your means describes spending more than you earn, which creates a gap that is usually filled with debt or savings drawn down.

ww.Saving half your income: Saving half your income is living well within your means, since you spend less than you earn; living beyond your means is the reverse.
ww.Spending exactly your income: Spending exactly your income is living at your means, with nothing left over; going beyond your means requires spending more than that amount.
ww.Investing in stocks and bonds: Investing in stocks and bonds is a way of putting money to work and is not by itself living beyond your means, which concerns overspending.

rw: Income of $2,800 minus expenses of $3,050 equals negative $250, so the budget has a $250 deficit because spending is higher than income.

ww.Break-even: Break-even needs income to equal expenses, but $2,800 is not equal to $3,050, so the budget does not balance.
ww.A $250 surplus: A surplus occurs when income exceeds expenses; here expenses of $3,050 are higher than income of $2,800, so it is a shortfall.
ww.A $5,850 surplus: $5,850 is the sum of income and expenses, which has no meaning in a budget; the difference, $250, shows a shortfall rather than a surplus.

rw: Income of $4,100 minus expenses of $3,650 equals $450, and since income is higher than spending, the budget shows a $450 surplus.

ww.Break-even: Break-even needs income to equal expenses, but $4,100 is more than $3,650, so the budget is not at break-even.
ww.A $7,750 surplus: $7,750 is the sum of income and expenses, which is meaningless here; the difference of the two figures is what shows a surplus or deficit.
ww.A $450 deficit: A deficit would mean expenses exceed income, but income of $4,100 is higher than expenses of $3,650, so the result is a surplus.

rw: Tracking income and spending for a month shows where your money actually goes, giving the real data needed to set up a workable budget.

ww.Cancel all savings and emergency funds: Cancelling savings and emergency funds removes your safety net and works against budgeting, which should include savings as a priority.
ww.Guess without records or any receipts: Guessing without records produces an unreliable budget, since your actual spending may differ widely from what you assume.
ww.Open several cards, so you can spend mor: Opening several cards to spend more adds debt risk and does not help you understand your spending, so it is not a good first step.

rw: An annual insurance premium comes only once a year as a large bill, which makes it irregular, so a budget should plan by setting money aside.

ww.Weekly grocery shopping: Weekly grocery shopping happens regularly, so it is a predictable ongoing cost and not an irregular expense that needs special planning.
ww.Daily coffee purchases: Daily coffee purchases are small and frequent, which makes them regular spending, not an irregular expense requiring special advance planning.
ww.Monthly rent payment: Monthly rent is a regular, fixed bill that arrives on a set schedule, so it is a predictable expense and not an irregular one.

rw: APR, or annual percentage rate, measures the yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage, including interest and certain fees, which lets you compare loans.

ww.The yearly earnings on savings at a bank: The yearly earnings on savings are described by APY or interest rate, not APR; APR measures the cost of borrowing on a loan.
ww.The monthly payment due on the loan each: The monthly payment depends on the amount, rate and term of the loan; APR is a yearly percentage rate and does not equal the payment.
ww.The credit score of the borrower on file: A borrower's credit score is a number from credit bureaus used by lenders; APR measures the cost of a loan, not the borrower.
